questions.stem:
A small mass is placed at point P on the inner surface of a smooth hemisphere as shown in the diagram below. It has an initial gravitational potential energy E and is released from rest at point P. The mass has a speed of 4.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ when it reaches the lowest point at T. Take the gravitational potential energy at T to be 0.

The diagram shows the speeds of the mass at points Q, R and S as it slides down.

Assuming air resistance is negligible, at which point does the mass possess 75% of its initial gravitational potential energy?
questions.stemText: A small mass is placed at point P on the inner surface of a smooth hemisphere as shown in the diagram below. It has an initial gravitational potential energy E and is released from rest at point P. The mass has a speed of 4.0 m s−1 when it reaches the lowest point at T. Take the gravitational potential energy at T to be 0. The diagram shows the speeds of the mass at points Q, R and S as it slides down. Assuming air resistance is negligible, at which point does the mass possess 75% of its initial gravitational potential energy? A Q B R C S D None of the points

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must infer the mass’s speed from the fraction of potential energy converted to kinetic energy.
questions.misconception: Assuming kinetic energy is proportional to speed

explanation.body: Let $r$ be the hemisphere’s radius. Conservation of energy between P and T gives $mgr=\tfrac12m(4.0)^2$, so $gr=8\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. When $75\%$ of the initial gravitational potential energy remains, $mgr=mg(3r/4)+\tfrac12mv^2$. This gives $v^2=gr/2$ and $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the speed at R.

perOption.A: Uses one-quarter of the final speed as though kinetic energy were proportional to speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses three-quarters of the final speed even though the remaining fraction refers to gravitational potential energy.
perOption.D: Overlooks that the calculated speed is listed at R.

questions.stem:
A motor with a constant output power pulls a wooden block vertically upwards from rest.

Which of the following graphs best represents the variation with time t of the speed v of the block?
questions.stemText: A motor with a constant output power pulls a wooden block vertically upwards from rest. Which of the following graphs best represents the variation with time t of the speed v of the block? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must link constant power to a falling pulling force and then to the gradient of the speed graph.
questions.misconception: Equating constant power with constant force.

explanation.body: At constant power $P$, the upward pulling force at speed $v$ is $P/v$. As the block speeds up, the pull decreases while its weight $mg$ stays constant, so the upward acceleration decreases. The speed approaches $P/(mg)$ as the pull approaches the weight.

perOption.A: Shows constant acceleration followed by a sudden drop to zero.
perOption.B: Shows constant acceleration throughout the rise.
perOption.C: Correct. The gradient gradually decreases as the pull approaches the weight.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration while the pulling force is falling.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A motor driving a pump raises $0.20\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of water through a vertical height of $10\ \mathrm{m}$ in $5.0$ minutes. The efficiency of the motor is 40% and the density of water is $1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

What is the power generated by the motor?

A $26\ \mathrm{W}$
B $65\ \mathrm{W}$
C $160\ \mathrm{W}$
D $9800\ \mathrm{W}$

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A motor driving a pump raises 0.20 m3 of water through a vertical height of 10 m in 5.0 minutes. The efficiency of the motor is 40% and the density of water is

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation links density, gravitational energy, elapsed time and efficiency.
questions.misconception: Multiplying useful output by efficiency to find input.

explanation.body: The useful power for lifting the water is $P=mg\Delta h/\Delta t=\rho Vg\Delta h/\Delta t$. Substituting gives $P=\frac{1000(0.20)(9.81)(10)}{5\times60}=65.4\ \mathrm{W}$. At 40% efficiency the required input power is $65.4/0.40=163.5\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $160\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies the useful lifting power by the efficiency.
perOption.B: Gives the useful lifting power before converting to input power.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the required input power.
perOption.D: Uses 5 seconds for the lifting time.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A small object of mass $m$ is launched by a spring and travels along a rough track to a point P as shown.

[The compressed spring is between a wall and the object at the left. The track dips by depth $H$ and rises to point P at the same height as the object’s starting position.]

The spring constant of the spring is $k$ and its initial compression is $x$.

As it travels to P, it goes through a distance $d$ and a dip of depth $H$. The object experiences a constant frictional force $f$ for the entire motion.

What is the kinetic energy of the object at point P?

A $\tfrac12kx^2-fd$
B $\tfrac12kx^2-fd-mgH$
C $\tfrac12kx^2+fd$
D $\tfrac12kx^2+fd+mgH$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: A small object of mass m is launched by a spring and travels along a rough track to a point P as shown. The spring constant of the spring is k and its initial c

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must track the frictional loss and compare the initial and final heights.
questions.misconception: Counting the dip depth as a net height change.

explanation.body: The object starts and finishes at the same height, so its gravitational potential energy is unchanged. The spring energy becomes kinetic energy and work done against friction, so $\tfrac12kx^2=(K_{\mathrm f}-K_{\mathrm i})+fd$. Since $K_{\mathrm i}=0$, $K_{\mathrm f}=\tfrac12kx^2-fd$.

perOption.A: Correct. Subtract the energy dissipated by friction from the initial spring energy.
perOption.B: Subtracts $mgH$ even though the object finishes at its starting height.
perOption.C: Adds $fd$ even though friction removes mechanical energy.
perOption.D: Adds the frictional loss and treats the dip as a net drop in height.

questions.stemText: A toy, of mass 0.22 kg, is released from rest on a smooth curved surface as shown. [Diagram: toy at the top of a smooth curved ramp, 40 cm above the flat bottom; the ramp levels out and leads to a horizontal spring fixed at the end.] It slides down the curved surface through a vertical distance of 40 cm and strikes a spring of force constant $350\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and compresses it a distance $x$ before coming to rest momentarily. Assuming no energy loss, what is the value of $x$? A $4.9\times10^{-3}$ m B $7.2\times10^{-3}$ m C $2.2\times10^{-2}$ m D $7.0\times10^{-2}$ m

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A toy, of mass 0.22 kg, is released from rest on a smooth curved surface as shown. It slides down the curved surface through a vertical distance of 40 cm and st

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single energy-conservation equation linking GPE to elastic PE.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square-root or forgetting the factor of 1/2 in elastic PE

explanation.body:
By conservation of energy, loss in GPE = gain in elastic potential energy:

$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgh}{k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.22)(9.81)(0.40)}{350}} = 7.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This is $x^2$: forgets to take the square root.
perOption.B: About what you get with $h = 0.40$ cm taken as $0.004$ m (factor-of-100 error in $h$).
perOption.C: Omits $g$ from $mgh$.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the resultant force to find the kinetic energy gain per second.
questions.misconception: Confusing engine output power with net mechanical power.

explanation.body: The rate of increase of kinetic energy is the net mechanical power, $F_{\mathrm{net}}v$. With $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, this gives $(250000)(0.90)(5.0)\ \mathrm{W}\approx1.1\ \mathrm{MW}$.

perOption.A: Calculates only the power dissipated by resistance.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the engine's total output power, including power dissipated by resistance.
perOption.D: Calculates the kinetic energy at that instant and reports it as a power.

What is the efficiency of the process?

A  $\frac{U}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$
B  $\frac{W}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$
C  $\frac{U}{W}\times100\%$
D  $\frac{U+W}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student only needs to identify the useful output and total input in the efficiency formula.

explanation.body: Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power, expressed as a percentage. Over the same time interval, the power ratio equals the energy ratio, giving $\frac{U}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$.

questions.stem:
A bungee jumper jumps from a platform and is decelerated by an elastic bungee cord, as shown.

When the jumper makes the jump, his initial gravitational potential energy is converted into his kinetic energy and into elastic potential energy in the cord.

At which part of the jump are all three types of energy non-zero?
questions.stemText: A bungee jumper jumps from a platform and is decelerated by an elastic bungee cord, as shown. NOT TO SCALE When the jumper makes the jump, his initial gravitational potential energy is converted into his kinetic energy and into elastic potential energy in the cord. At which part of the jump are all three types of energy non-zero? A On the platform before the jump. B On the way down before the cord has started to extend. C On the way down when the net force acting on the jumper is zero. D At the point when the cord is stretched to a maximum.

options.label: A
options.text: On the platform before the jump.

options.label: B
options.text: On the way down before the cord has started to extend.

options.label: C
options.text: On the way down when the net force acting on the jumper is zero.

options.label: D
options.text: At the point when the cord is stretched to a maximum.

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must track the jumper’s height, speed and cord extension at each stage.
questions.misconception: Equating zero net force with zero speed

explanation.body: Before the jump the jumper is stationary and the cord is slack. On the way down before the cord extends, its elastic potential energy is still zero. When the net force is zero on the way down, the jumper is above ground and moving, and the cord is stretched, so all three energies are nonzero. At maximum extension the jumper is momentarily at rest.

perOption.A: The stationary jumper and slack cord give zero kinetic and elastic potential energy.
perOption.B: The cord is still slack, so its elastic potential energy is zero.
perOption.C: Correct. The jumper is moving above ground with the cord stretched.
perOption.D: The jumper momentarily stops, so kinetic energy is zero.

The solid line on the graph shows how the length of a rubber band varies when an increasing load is applied. The dotted line shows how the length subsequently varies as the load is gradually decreased.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: The solid line on the graph shows how the length of a rubber band varies when an increasing load is applied. The dotted line shows how the length subsequently varies as the load is gradually decreased. Which statement is correct? A The energy recovered when the load is removed is about 10 J. B The energy remaining in the rubber band after one cycle of loading and unloading is about 3 J. C The total work done on the rubber band during one cycle of loading and unloading is about 14 J. D The work done in stretching the rubber band is about 5 J.

options.label: A
options.text: The energy recovered when the load is removed is about 10 J.

options.label: B
options.text: The energy remaining in the rubber band after one cycle of loading and unloading is about 3 J.

options.label: C
options.text: The total work done on the rubber band during one cycle of loading and unloading is about 14 J.

options.label: D
options.text: The work done in stretching the rubber band is about 5 J.

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must estimate the areas under both curves and take their difference.
questions.misconception: Treating energy lost in hysteresis as recoverable elastic energy

explanation.body: The key estimates the work done stretching the band as $\tfrac12(0.5)(35)\approx9\ \mathrm{J}$ and the energy recovered as $\tfrac12(0.6)(20)=6\ \mathrm{J}$. The net work in one cycle is about $9-6=3\ \mathrm{J}$. Counting about six squares between the curves also gives $(5\times0.1)\times6=3\ \mathrm{J}$, the quantity the key calls the energy remaining.

perOption.A: The unloading area gives about 6 J of recovered energy.
perOption.B: Correct in the key’s intended sense of net work over the cycle.
perOption.C: Net work is the loading area minus the unloading area, about 3 J.
perOption.D: The loading area gives about 9 J of work during stretching.

questions.misconception: Assuming constant force gives constant power

explanation.body: A constant force gives a constant acceleration $a$. Since the body starts from rest, $v=u+at=at$. Thus $P=Fv=Fat$, so power increases linearly from zero.

perOption.A: Assumes constant force gives constant power even while speed increases.

questions.stemText:
The gravitational field strength on the surface of planet P is one tenth of that on the surface of planet Q.

On the surface of P, a body has a mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and a weight of $1.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

What are the mass and weight of the same body on the surface of planet Q?

|   | mass on Q / kg | weight on Q / N |
|---|---:|---:|
| A | 1.0 | 0.1 |
| B | 1.0 | 10 |
| C | 10 | 10 |
| D | 10 | 100 |

stemImage.alt: Question 11: The gravitational field strength on the surface of planet P is one tenth of that on the surface of planet Q. On the surface of P, a body has a mass of 1.0 kg an

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must keep mass fixed and multiply weight by the field-strength ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating mass as dependent on local gravity

explanation.body: On P, $g_P=W_P/m=1.0/1.0=1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. On Q, $g_Q=10g_P=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and the mass is still $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. The weight on Q is therefore $W_Q=1.0(10)=10\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field-strength ratio and divides the weight by ten.
perOption.B: Correct. The same mass weighs 10 N in the stronger field.
perOption.C: Scales up the mass even though the weight is correctly estimated.
perOption.D: Scales up both the mass and field strength, applying the same factor twice.

questions.stem:
An old-fashioned 60 W lamp converts 95% of its energy supply into heat. A 4.0 W modern lamp has the same power output of light as the old-fashioned lamp.

What is the efficiency of the modern lamp?
questions.stemText: An old-fashioned 60 W lamp converts 95% of its energy supply into heat. A 4.0 W modern lamp has the same power output of light as the old-fashioned lamp. What is the efficiency of the modern lamp? A 5.0% B 6.7% C 75% D 95%

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two-step efficiency calculation using useful light power.
questions.misconception: Confusing heat output percentage with efficiency

explanation.body: The old lamp’s useful light output is $60(100-95)/100=3.0\ \mathrm{W}$. The modern lamp produces the same light output with a $4.0\ \mathrm{W}$ input, so its efficiency is $(3.0/4.0)\times100\%=75\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the old lamp’s efficiency.
perOption.B: Divides the modern lamp’s input power by the old lamp’s input power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the fraction of the old lamp’s input converted to heat.

The weight is at rest. 30 cm 40 cm weight of 2 N What is the potential energy stored in the spring? A 0.1 J B 0.2 J C 0.6 J D 0.8 J

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Uses the extension and accounts for the increasing spring force.
questions.misconception: Using the full length as the extension

explanation.body: By Hooke's law, $F=ke$, with extension $e=0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. The stored energy is $\frac12ke^2=\frac12Fe=\frac12(2)(0.10)=0.1\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The energy is half the final force times the extension.
perOption.B: Uses the final force over the full extension and misses the factor of one-half.
perOption.C: Multiplies the final force by the unstretched length.
perOption.D: Multiplies the final force by the stretched length.

questions.stem:
A car with a power output of 100 kW is travelling with a constant speed of 30 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ along a straight road. The frictional force on the car is proportional to the square of its speed.

What constant speed will it be travelling at if its power output is 200 kW?
questions.stemText: A car with a power output of 100 kW is travelling with a constant speed of 30 m s-1 along a straight road. The frictional force on the car is proportional to the square of its speed. What constant speed will it be travelling at if its power output is 200 kW? A 37.8 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 42.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 51.6 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 60.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Combines force balance with the additional speed factor in power.
questions.misconception: Assuming power scales like friction

explanation.body: At constant speed the resultant force is zero, so the driving force balances friction, $F=kv^2$. Using $P=Fv=kv^3$ gives $\frac{100}{30^3}=\frac{200}{v^3}$. Hence $v=2^{1/3}(30)=37.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Doubling power multiplies speed by the cube root of two.
perOption.B: Uses square-root scaling and misses the extra speed factor in power.
perOption.C: Overestimates the speed increase and would require about five times the original power.
perOption.D: Doubles the speed as though power were directly proportional to speed.

questions.misconception: Confusing cumulative work with force

explanation.body: Since $W=\int F\,\mathrm{d}s$, the force is the gradient of the work–displacement graph. The gradient starts at zero, increases, is briefly approximately constant, then falls to zero at the maximum work. The work then decreases, so the force is negative.

perOption.A: Shows an initially constant positive force even though the work gradient starts at zero and increases.
perOption.B: Correct. The force follows the gradient and becomes negative after the maximum.
perOption.C: Omits the negative force needed for work to decrease.
perOption.D: Copies the work curve and stays positive where the gradient is negative.

A driving force of 1.6 kN is produced by the car engine on the wheels to keep the car moving at a constant speed of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on level road.

The total energy of the fuel consumed by the engine is 1.8 MJ per minute.

What is the efficiency of the car in converting the energy of the fuel into useful work done on the car to keep it moving at the constant speed of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on level ground?

A 20 % B 33 % C 36 % D 59 %

questions.difficultyReason: Two-step: useful power from P = Fv, then input power from energy per minute.

perOption.A: Underestimates the ratio of the $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful power to the $30.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ fuel input.
perOption.B: At the stated fuel input, this percentage accounts for only about $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ of useful power.
perOption.C: This percentage treats the roughly $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful output as only a little over a third of the $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ input.

questions.stemText:
Which row in the table gives the gravitational potential energy, the elastic potential energy and the kinetic energy of a bungee jumper during the first fall? Air resistance is negligible.

| | | gravitational potential energy / kJ | elastic potential energy / kJ | kinetic energy / kJ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | top | 120 | 0 | 0 |
| | middle | 60 | 10 | 50 |
| | bottom | 0 | 120 | 0 |
| B | top | 120 | 0 | 0 |
| | middle | 60 | 30 | 30 |
| | bottom | 0 | 60 | 60 |
| C | top | 120 | 0 | 0 |
| | middle | 60 | 30 | 60 |
| | bottom | 0 | 120 | 0 |
| D | top | 120 | 0 | 0 |
| | middle | 60 | 60 | 0 |
| | bottom | 0 | 120 | 0 |

stemImage.alt: Question 5: Which row in the table gives the gravitational potential energy, the elastic potential energy and the kinetic energy of a bungee jumper during the first fall? A

appearances.originalFile: grail:14599 (VJC) 2024 H2 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires checking conservation of total energy and the zero-KE condition at the lowest point.
questions.misconception: Maximum speed occurs at the lowest point

explanation.body:
At the top there is only gravitational potential energy, so elastic PE and KE are both 0.

At the bottom all the GPE has been converted to elastic PE and the jumper is momentarily at rest, so KE = 0 (B is wrong).

At the middle the GPE lost is converted into both elastic PE and KE; the jumper is still moving, so KE cannot be 0 (D is wrong).

The total energy stays constant at 120 kJ (C is wrong, as its middle row adds to 150 kJ). Only A fits.

perOption.A: Correct. Total is 120 kJ at every point, KE is 0 at the top and bottom, and non-zero in the middle.
perOption.B: At the bottom the jumper is momentarily at rest, so KE must be 0 and all 120 kJ is elastic PE.
perOption.C: The middle row totals 60 + 30 + 60 = 150 kJ, breaking conservation of energy.
perOption.D: The jumper is still moving at the middle, so KE cannot be 0.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An escalator is 60 m long and lifts passengers through a vertical height of 30 m, as shown.

To drive the escalator against the forces of friction when there are no passengers requires a power of 2.0 kW. The escalator is used by passengers of average mass 60 kg and the power to overcome friction remains constant. How much power is required to drive the escalator when it is carrying 20 passengers and is travelling at 0.75 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$?
questions.stemText: An escalator is 60 m long and lifts passengers through a vertical height of 30 m, as shown. 30 m 60 m To drive the escalator against the forces of friction when there are no passengers requires a power of 2.0 kW. The escalator is used by passengers of average mass 60 kg and the power to overcome friction remains constant. How much power is required to drive the escalator when it is carrying 20 passengers and is travelling at 0.75 m s-1? A 4.4 kW B 6.4 kW C 8.8 kW D 10.8 kW

appearances.originalFile: grail:14599 (VJC) 2024 H2 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires resolving weight along the incline, using $P = Fv$, and adding the constant friction power.
questions.misconception: Using the full weight rather than its component along the slope

explanation.body:
Power needed = power with no passengers + power to lift 20 passengers of average mass 60 kg.

$P = P_{\text{escalator}} + Fv = P_{\text{escalator}} + (mg\sin\theta)v$, where $\sin\theta = \frac{30}{60}$.

$P = 2.0 \times 10^{3} + 20(60)(9.81)\left(\frac{30}{60}\right)(0.75) = 6414\ \mathrm{W} \approx 6.4\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Leaves out the 2.0 kW needed to overcome friction (gives only 4.4 kW for the passengers).
perOption.B: Correct. 2.0 kW + 4.4 kW for lifting the passengers.
perOption.C: Uses the full weight times the speed along the slope, missing the factor $\sin\theta$, and also leaves out friction.
perOption.D: Misses the factor $\sin\theta = 30/60$, using $mgv$ instead of $mgv\sin\theta$.

questions.stem: A speed boat has two identical motors. When both motors are working, the speed boat attained a maximum speed of 36.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Given that the drag force on the speed boat is proportional to the square of the speed, what is the maximum speed of the boat when only one motor is working?
questions.stemText: A speed boat has two identical motors. When both motors are working, the speed boat attained a maximum speed of 36.0 m s−1. Given that the drag force on the speed boat is proportional to the square of the speed, what is the maximum speed of the boat when only one motor is working? A 9.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 18.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 24.2 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 28.6 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires combining P = Fv with drag ∝ v² to get P ∝ v³, then a cube-root ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming maximum speed is proportional to power

explanation.body:
Power output $P = F_{\text{driving}}v$. At maximum speed the driving force equals the drag force, $F_{\text{driving}} = kv^2$, so $P = (kv^2)v = kv^3$.

Hence $\dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{v_1^3}{v_2^3}$. With one motor, $P_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}P_2$:

$\sqrt[3]{\tfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{v_1}{36}$, so $v_1 = 28.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides by 4, as if speed were inversely proportional to the square of the power ratio.
perOption.B: Halves the speed, assuming speed is proportional to power.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong power law; with drag $\propto v^2$, power $\propto v^3$.
perOption.D: Correct. $P \propto v^3$, so $v = 36/\sqrt[3]{2}$.

What is the spring constant of the spring?
questions.stemText: A 20 g ball bearing is released from rest 10 cm above the top of an unstretched spring. It compresses the spring and comes to rest when the spring is compressed by 2.4 cm as shown in the figure below. 10 cm 2.4 cm What is the spring constant of the spring? A 2.0 N m $^{-1}$ B 8.6 N m $^{-1}$ C 68 N m $^{-1}$ D 84 N m $^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Straightforward energy conservation, but students often forget the extra compression distance in the GPE term.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the extra drop during compression

explanation.body:
Loss in GPE = gain in elastic potential energy. The ball falls through $h + x$, not just $h$:

$mg(h+x) = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

$(0.020)(9.81)(0.10 + 0.024) = \tfrac{1}{2}k(0.024)^2$

$k = 84\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Does not follow from the energy balance; likely a unit or arithmetic slip.
perOption.B: Treats the final position as static equilibrium ($mg = kx$), but the ball is momentarily at rest, not in equilibrium.
perOption.C: Uses a fall height of only 10 cm, ignoring the extra 2.4 cm fall while compressing the spring.
perOption.D: Correct. $mg(h+x) = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

A man pulls a rope attached to a sled. The rope makes an angle of $30^{\mathrm{o}}$ with the horizontal. The man exerts a force of 20.0 N on the rope to move the sled horizontally through a distance of 40 m.

What is the work done by the man?
questions.stemText: A man pulls a rope attached to a sled. The rope makes an angle of 30o with the horizontal. The man exerts a force of 20.0 N on the rope to move the sled horizontally through a distance of 40 m. What is the work done by the man? A 400 J B 490 J C 690 J D 800 J

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation uses the component of a given force along a given displacement.
questions.misconception: Using the full pulling force for horizontal work.

explanation.body: Work is the component of the pulling force along the sled’s motion multiplied by the distance moved. Thus $W=(20.0\cos 30^\circ)(40)\approx692.8\ \mathrm{J}$, which rounds to $690\ \mathrm{J}$ at the precision of the options.

perOption.A: Uses the vertical component $20.0sin30^circ$ for horizontal motion.
perOption.B: Uses an effective horizontal force of about $12.3 mathrm{N}$, below the actual $20.0cos30^circ$.
perOption.C: Correct. Only the horizontal force component does work on the sled.
perOption.D: Uses the full $20.0 mathrm{N}$ without projecting it along the displacement.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish extension from total length and find the area against the correct axis.

explanation.body: The spring length increases from $7.5$ to $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ while the force increases from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm{N}$. The work is the trapezoidal area between the line and the length axis over that interval. This gives $W=\tfrac12(3.0+6.0)(10.0-7.5)\times10^{-2}=0.11\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct. The trapezoid uses the initial and final forces over the extra extension.
perOption.B: Uses the final force of 6.0 N throughout the extra extension.
perOption.C: Takes the area against the force axis using the mean length and the change in force.
perOption.D: Takes the entire trapezoid against the force axis from 0 to 6.0 N.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: Which statement is correct? A A ball lands on the ground and bounces. The kinetic energy changes sign because the ball changes direction. B A car drives up a rough slope at steady speed. The power generated by the engine equals the gravitational potential energy gained per unit time. C It is possible for an electric heater to be 100% efficient. D It is impossible for momentum to be conserved in a collision.

options.label: A
options.text: A ball lands on the ground and bounces. The kinetic energy changes sign because the ball changes direction.

options.label: B
options.text: A car drives up a rough slope at steady speed. The power generated by the engine equals the gravitational potential energy gained per unit time.

options.label: C
options.text: It is possible for an electric heater to be 100% efficient.

options.label: D
options.text: It is impossible for momentum to be conserved in a collision.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Each statement tests a basic energy or momentum fact.
questions.misconception: Believing no device can ever be 100% efficient

explanation.body:
C: An electric heater's purpose is to produce thermal energy, and all the electrical energy input can end up as thermal energy, so it can be 100% efficient.

A: The velocity changes direction on bouncing, but kinetic energy has no direction and stays positive.

B: The engine's power equals the gravitational potential energy gained per unit time plus the rate of work done against friction.

D: Momentum must be conserved in a collision (for an isolated system).

perOption.A: Kinetic energy is a scalar and is never negative; only velocity changes sign.
perOption.B: Ignores the rate of work done against friction on the rough slope.
perOption.C: Correct. All the electrical energy can be converted to the desired thermal energy.
perOption.D: Momentum is always conserved in a collision of an isolated system.

questions.difficultyReason: Simple recognition that horizontal motion does no work against a vertical field.

explanation.body:
Moving at right angles to a vertical gravitational field means the object stays at the same level as before.

Since the field is uniform, there is no change in the gravitational potential energy of the object.

perOption.A: GPE decreases only if the object moves down, along the field.
perOption.B: Correct. No displacement along the field, so no work is done by gravity.
perOption.C: GPE increases only with an upward displacement against the field.
perOption.D: No dependence on horizontal displacement at all in a uniform vertical field.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Read the limit of proportionality off the graph and find a triangle's area, remembering the natural length offset.
questions.misconception: Using length instead of extension

explanation.body:
Hooke's law holds along the straight-line section, up to a length of 40 mm where $F = 70\ \mathrm{N}$. The extension is measured from the natural length of 20 mm.

$EPE = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2}(70)(0.040 - 0.020) = 0.70\ \mathrm{J}$

perOption.A: Unit-conversion slip in the extension.
perOption.B: Correct. Area under the linear section: $\frac{1}{2}(70)(0.020)$.
perOption.C: Forgets the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ (uses $Fx$ instead of the triangle area).
perOption.D: Leaves the extension in mm instead of converting to m.

explanation.body:
Useful work done in lifting the weight $= (480)(3.5) = 1680\ \mathrm{J}$.

Work done by the man pulling the rope $= (200)(10.5) = 2100\ \mathrm{J}$.

Efficiency $= \frac{1680}{2100}\times100\% = 80\%$

perOption.A: Does not follow from useful output over input work.
perOption.B: Does not follow from useful output over input work.
perOption.C: Does not follow from useful output over input work.

questions.stemText: An electric motor is required to haul a cage of mass 400 kg up a mine shaft through a vertical height of 1200 m in 2.0 minutes. What will be the electrical power required if the overall efficiency is 80%? A 3.2 kW B 4.9 kW C 32 kW D 49 kW

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting minutes to seconds and applying efficiency to the power balance.
questions.misconception: Multiplying useful power by efficiency.

explanation.body: The electrical input power multiplied by efficiency equals the gain in gravitational potential energy per unit time. Thus $P_\mathrm{in}=\frac{400\times9.81\times1200}{120}\div0.80=49\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Uses the efficiency factor in the wrong direction and is about a factor of ten below even that estimate.
perOption.B: Underestimates the correctly efficiency-adjusted power by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Multiplies the useful power by efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.
